title: vLLM attention backends: selection, batching, KV layout, CUDA graphs
summary: How vLLM plugs FlashAttention, FlashInfer, Triton, FlashMLA and CPU kernels behind one interface: priority-based selection, mixed prefill/decode batches, KV layouts and CUDA graph limits.
outcomes: Explain the roles of AttentionBackend, AttentionMetadataBuilder and AttentionImpl in one vLLM step
Predict which backend vLLM selects for a given GPU, model and flags, and why an explicit choice can fail
Trace how a mixed prefill/decode batch is reordered, split and handed to different kernels
Compute KV page bytes, block table sizes, slot numbers and CUDA graph padding for a configuration
Explain how AttentionCGSupport limits CUDA graph modes and when vLLM downgrades them

lessons.title: One attention layer, many kernels: the backend abstraction

blocks.md:
vLLM runs on Ampere, Hopper and Blackwell GPUs, on AMD GPUs and on CPUs. It serves models with grouped-query attention (GQA), DeepSeek-style multi-head latent attention (MLA), sliding windows and attention sinks, with KV caches in BF16 or FP8. No single attention kernel covers that whole space.

The source is explicit about the limits. The FlashMLA backend accepts only compute capability (NVIDIA's GPU architecture version: 8.x Ampere, 9.x Hopper, 10.x data-center Blackwell) 9.x or 10.x and a kernel block size of exactly 64. `CUTLASS_MLA` accepts only 10.x and blocks of 128. `TRITON_ATTN` accepts any compute capability, which makes it the usual fallback. So vLLM separates *what* a layer computes (attention over a paged KV cache) from *how* (a pluggable **attention backend**).

You already know the *what* from the prerequisites. PagedAttention stores KV in fixed-size blocks reached through a per-request block table. FlashAttention-style kernels tile the computation so scores never touch HBM. A backend is the glue that feeds vLLM's block tables into one such kernel.

A backend in vLLM (`vllm/v1/attention/backend.py`) has three parts:

1. `AttentionBackend`: a class with no per-step state. It names itself (`get_name`) and declares what it supports: model dtypes, KV cache dtypes, kernel block sizes, head sizes, compute capability, MLA or not, sinks, sliding window. It also returns the other two classes.
2. `AttentionMetadataBuilder`: runs once per step for each KV cache group. It turns the shared batch description into the tensors this kernel wants.
3. `AttentionImpl`: one instance per layer. Its `forward(layer, query, key, value, kv_cache, attn_metadata, output)` writes the result into `output`.

blocks.title: One decode step through an attention backend

nodes.label:
Metadata builder
(one per KV cache group)

scenes.caption: The scheduler says how many tokens each request runs this step. Nothing backend-specific has happened yet.
The runner flattens the batch into one token list and fills CommonAttentionMetadata: query_start_loc, seq_lens, block_table_tensor, slot_mapping. Every backend gets this same description.

The chosen backend's builder turns the shared description into its own metadata once per step, for example FlashAttention scheduler data or FlashInfer plans. This is the only per-step backend-specific setup.

Every attention layer reuses that one metadata object. Each layer's impl writes the new K and V into the paged cache at the slots in slot_mapping, then calls the kernel that reads the blocks back through the block table.

blocks.md:
The shared input, `CommonAttentionMetadata`, carries what any paged kernel needs. Its main fields are:

- `query_start_loc` with shape (batch + 1): where each request's new tokens start in the flattened token list.
- `seq_lens`: the total length of each request after this step (cached context plus new tokens).
- `num_reqs`, `num_actual_tokens`, `max_query_len`, `max_seq_len`.
- `block_table_tensor`: the per-request block tables from PagedAttention.
- `slot_mapping`: for each new token, the flat cache slot its K and V go into.

blocks.caption: Shape of an out-of-tree backend. The names (register_backend, the CUSTOM placeholder, MultipleOf, AttentionCGSupport) are taken from vLLM main; method bodies are elided.

blocks.md:
Two builder class attributes come back in later lessons. `reorder_batch_threshold` asks the runner to move short requests (decodes) to the front of the batch. `_cudagraph_support` says which batches this backend can run inside a captured CUDA graph.

The registry is `AttentionBackendEnum` in `vllm/v1/attention/backends/registry.py`. Each member's value is a class path, for example `FLASH_ATTN`, `FLASHINFER`, `TRITON_ATTN`, `FLEX_ATTENTION`, `FLASHMLA`, `CUTLASS_MLA`, `FLASHINFER_MLA`, `TRITON_MLA`, `FLASH_ATTN_MLA`, `ROCM_ATTN`, `CPU_ATTN` and `CPU_MLA`. A `CUSTOM` placeholder lets plugins register their own.

A backend is mostly a *declaration*: what it supports, plus two factories. Selection, batching, KV layout and CUDA graph capture are all driven by those declarations, so a backend never needs to know about the scheduler.

blocks.question: A model has 32 attention layers that all use the same backend and one KV cache group. In one engine step, how many times does that backend's metadata builder run `build()`?
options: Once, and all 32 layers reuse the result
32 times, once per layer, because each layer has its own KV cache
Once per request in the batch
Zero times on decode steps, because decode metadata is cached
blocks.explain: The builder runs once per step per KV cache group, and the layers in that group share the metadata object. Per-layer work happens in `AttentionImpl.forward`. That is why `forward` must stay cheap on the CPU.

blocks.question: Which piece declares that a backend needs compute capability 8.0 or higher?
options: The `AttentionImpl` instance, by checking the GPU inside `forward`
The metadata builder, by raising during `build()`
The `AttentionBackend` class, through `supports_compute_capability`, which selection calls before anything runs
The scheduler, which skips requests on unsupported GPUs
blocks.explain: Capabilities live on the backend class so they can be checked at startup. `validate_configuration` calls `supports_compute_capability` along with the head size, dtype, KV dtype and block size checks.

lessons.title: How vLLM chooses a backend: priority lists and validation

blocks.md: At startup each attention layer calls `get_attn_backend` in `vllm/v1/attention/selector.py`. That function packs the layer's facts into an `AttentionSelectorConfig`: head size, model dtype, KV cache dtype, block size (only if you pinned `--block-size`), MLA or not, sinks, sparse, sliding window, and more. The platform's `get_attn_backend_cls` then picks a class.

On CUDA the rule (`vllm/platforms/cuda.py`) is short:

1. If you named a backend, validate only that one. If it fails, raise `ValueError` with the reasons. There is no silent fallback.
2. Otherwise take the priority list for this GPU and attention type. Run `validate_configuration` on every entry and keep the valid ones.
3. Pick the valid backend with the best priority. Log the full list of valid candidates.
4. If nothing is valid, raise an error that lists every backend and why it failed.

blocks.title: Walking the CUDA priority list (standard attention)

nodes.label:
Selector config
head size, dtypes, block size

scenes.caption: On any GPU that is not compute capability 10.x, the standard list is FLASH_ATTN, FLASHINFER, TRITON_ATTN, FLEX_ATTENTION, TURBOQUANT. Each entry is checked against the same selector config.
H100 (SM 9.0), BF16 model, head size 128, block size not pinned. FLASH_ATTN validates, and on Hopper it defaults to FlashAttention-3. Priority 1 wins.

T4 (SM 7.5), FP16 model. FLASH_ATTN needs capability 8.0 or higher, and FLASHINFER is currently limited to 8.0 through 12.1. TRITON_ATTN accepts any capability and head sizes of 32 or more, so it wins.

On compute capability 10.x (data-center Blackwell) with causal attention, the list puts FLASHINFER first (its TRTLLM kernels), then FLASH_ATTN. If you set non-causal attention, FLASH_ATTN goes back to the front.
Back on the T4: --attention-backend FLASHINFER skips the list. Only FLASHINFER is validated, it fails the capability check, and startup stops with a ValueError naming the reason.

blocks.md:
MLA models (`use_mla=True`) use separate lists. On compute capability 10.x the dense part starts `FLASHINFER_MLA`, `TOKENSPEED_MLA`, `CUTLASS_MLA`, `FLASH_ATTN_MLA`, `FLASHMLA`, `TRITON_MLA`. On other capabilities, 9.x included, it starts `FLASH_ATTN_MLA`, `FLASHMLA`, `FLASHINFER_MLA`, `TRITON_MLA`. On 12.x the list is `TRITON_MLA` and then a sparse backend. Sparse MLA entries come after the dense ones, and their order depends on the KV dtype and head count.

MLA has two halves. The backend above handles decode. Prefill is chosen separately (`-ac.mla_prefill_backend`, with options such as `FLASH_ATTN`, `FLASHINFER` and `TRTLLM_RAGGED`), automatically by default.

Other platforms have their own logic. On CPU, standard attention always gets `CPU_ATTN`. MLA gets `AMX_MLA` when the x86 CPU has AMX tiles, and `CPU_MLA` otherwise.

blocks.code:
# simple form
vllm serve Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B --attention-backend FLASH_ATTN

# structured form (mutually exclusive with the flag above)
vllm serve Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B -ac.backend FLASH_ATTN
vllm serve Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B -ac '{"backend": "FLASH_ATTN", "flash_attn_version": 2}'

# Python
from vllm import LLM
llm = LLM(model="Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B", attention_backend="FLASH_ATTN")
blocks.caption: Ways to pin a backend, from the vLLM attention backends design doc. flash_attn_version accepts 2, 3 or 4.

blocks.md: Older guides set the `VLLM_ATTENTION_BACKEND` environment variable. It existed in `vllm/envs.py` up to the v0.14 release and is gone from main. Use `--attention-backend` or `--attention-config` (`-ac`). `AttentionConfig.backend_per_kind` can also set a backend per KV cache group kind, for example a different one for sliding-window MLA layers.

Two smaller rules matter in practice. FlashAttention picks its version by GPU: FA3 on compute capability 9.x, FA4 on 10.x when it is installed, and FA2 otherwise. You can override this with `flash_attn_version`. And if you pin `--block-size` without pinning a backend, a higher-priority backend may be rejected only because of the block size. vLLM then logs a warning that `--block-size` precluded those backends and suggests removing the flag.
Automatic selection takes the first backend in the platform's priority list that passes `validate_configuration`. Explicit selection validates one backend and fails loudly. Neither path guesses.

blocks.question: On an A100 (SM 8.0) you start a BF16 model with `--attention-backend FLASHMLA`. The model is not MLA. What happens?
options: vLLM ignores the flag and uses FLASH_ATTN, the first valid entry
Startup fails with a ValueError listing reasons such as compute capability not supported and non-MLA not supported
FLASHMLA runs, but more slowly than FLASH_ATTN
vLLM switches to TRITON_MLA because it accepts any GPU
blocks.explain: An explicit backend is validated alone. FLASHMLA reports `is_mla()` as true and accepts only capability 9.x or 10.x, so `validate_configuration` returns reasons and `get_attn_backend_cls` raises. The design doc shows this same error format.

blocks.question: On a B200 serving a DeepSeek-style MLA model you pinned `--block-size 16`. The log warns that `--block-size 16 precluded higher-priority backend(s) FLASHINFER_MLA, CUTLASS_MLA, FLASHMLA`. FLASHINFER_MLA supports block sizes 32 and 64. What fixes it?
options: Keep the flag and add `--attention-backend FLASHINFER_MLA`
Set `VLLM_ATTENTION_BACKEND=FLASHINFER_MLA`
Raise `--gpu-memory-utilization` so the larger blocks fit
Remove `--block-size` (or pin 32 or 64), so FLASHINFER_MLA passes validation and wins on priority
blocks.explain: A pinned block size goes into the selector config, and `supports_block_size` rejects 16 because it is not a multiple of 32 or 64. Forcing the backend while keeping 16 fails validation with a ValueError. The environment variable no longer exists. Removing the pin lets vLLM use the backend's preferred size.

lessons.title: Mixed prefill and decode in one forward pass

blocks.md: vLLM V1 has no separate prefill and decode steps. Each step the scheduler hands out a token budget, and one forward pass can mix requests that decode one token, requests that continue a chunked prefill, and brand-new prompts. The runner flattens all their new tokens into one list. `query_start_loc` marks where each request's tokens begin, and `seq_lens` holds each request's total length after this step.

Our running example has five requests:

- A, C and E are decoding: their prompts are done (40, 17 and 60 tokens computed) and each runs 1 token.
- D is a chunked prefill: 32 of its 50 prompt tokens are cached, and it runs 5 more.
- B is new: 0 tokens computed, and it runs its whole 6-token prompt.

That is 14 tokens in total, in arrival order A, B, C, D, E.

scenes.caption: Arrival order, flattened into 14 tokens. query_start_loc = [0, 1, 7, 8, 13, 14]. FlashAttention can consume this exactly as it is.

Classify each request: decode (has context, at most threshold tokens, prompt done), short extend, long extend (has context, more than threshold) or prefill (no context yet). A, C, E are decodes, D is a long extend and B is a pure prefill.
reorder_batch_to_split_decodes_and_prefills swaps states so the order is decode, short extend, long extend, prefill. Only B and E needed to swap. Decodes now occupy tokens 0 to 2.
The metadata now reads query_start_loc = [0, 1, 2, 3, 8, 14] and seq_lens = [41, 61, 18, 37, 6]. One integer, num_decode_tokens = 3, splits the batch for backends that need two kernels.

blocks.md: The runner only reorders when some builder asks for it. It takes the **minimum** `reorder_batch_threshold` over all attention groups, and `None` means no reordering. After the reorder, `split_decodes_and_prefills` finds the boundary. It treats requests with a query length at or below the threshold as decodes, and with `require_uniform` set, it also needs every decode to have the same length.

Backends then go different ways:

- **FLASH_ATTN** sets no threshold. It makes one variable-length kernel call over all 14 tokens, with `cu_seqlens_q = query_start_loc`, `seqused_k = seq_lens` and the block table. Each query row attends causally to its own request's pages.
- **FLASHINFER** uses threshold 1. It runs a decode kernel on `output[:3]` and a prefill kernel on `output[3:]`.
- **MLA backends** split into two math paths. Decode tokens go through `forward_mqa`, which works on the 576-wide compressed latent like multi-query attention. Prefill tokens go through `forward_mha`, which first expands the latent into per-head K and V. `FLASHMLA` uses threshold 128 with uniform decodes. `FLASH_ATTN_MLA` uses threshold 512 and accepts mixed lengths, so short prefills take the decode path.

blocks.prompt: Same 14-token batch, now on a DeepSeek-style MLA model with FLASH_ATTN_MLA (threshold 512, variable-length decode). How many tokens go to the decode path?
blocks.reveal:
All **14**. In `split_decodes_and_prefills`, `max_query_len` is 6, which is at most 512, and uniformity is not required, so every request counts as a decode, even B's fresh prompt. The source says this on purpose: *process small prefills with decode pathway*.

With FLASHMLA (threshold 128, uniform), A, E and C have length 1, while D (5) and B (6) do not match, so the split is 3 decode tokens and 11 prefill tokens.

blocks.title: Where the 14 tokens go, by backend

scenes.caption: FLASH_ATTN: one kernel handles decodes and prefills together, so no split is needed.
FLASHINFER (threshold 1): the 3 single-token decodes go to the decode kernel, and D's 5 plus B's 6 go to the prefill kernel.
FLASHMLA (threshold 128, uniform decodes): D and B have lengths 5 and 6, not 1, so the split matches FlashInfer.
FLASH_ATTN_MLA (threshold 512, variable length): the whole batch takes the latent-space MQA path.

blocks.md: Writing new K and V uses `slot_mapping`. For a token at position $p$ in a request with block table $T$ and block size $B$:

blocks.caption: Example: T = [7, 1, 3] and B = 16. Position 37 is in logical block 2 at offset 5, so its slot is 3 x 16 + 5 = 53. Position 16 maps to slot 16 and position 0 to slot 112. Padded token rows get PAD_SLOT_ID = -1, so no real slot is written.

blocks.md: A mixed batch is one flat list of tokens plus offsets. Backends with one variable-length kernel use it as is. Backends with separate decode and prefill kernels ask for decodes first, so one index splits the batch.

blocks.question: Request D has 32 of its 50 prompt tokens computed and is scheduled for 5 tokens. Under threshold 1, where does the reorder put it?
options: In the long-extend region, after any short extends and before the fresh prefills
With the decodes, since it already has context
At the very end with the pure prefills, since its prompt is not finished
It is not reordered, because only new requests move
blocks.explain: It has context (32 > 0) and runs more tokens than the threshold (5 > 1), so it is a long extend. The order is decode, short extend, long extend, prefill. Pure prefill means no computed tokens at all, which describes B.

blocks.question: A model mixes a backend that reports `reorder_batch_threshold = 1` with one that reports `None`. Does the runner reorder?
options: No, because None disables reordering for everyone
Yes, but each backend gets its own differently ordered copy of the batch
Yes, with threshold 1. The runner takes the minimum and ignores None
Only on steps that contain no prefills
blocks.explain: `calculate_reorder_batch_threshold` reduces with a min that skips None. One batch order is shared by all layers, so the smallest threshold wins, and backends that need no order are unaffected.

lessons.title: KV cache layout and block sizes per backend

blocks.md:
Every backend reads the same paged cache, but kernels care about *byte order* inside it. vLLM describes a layer's page logically as $[B, H, N, C]$: blocks, KV head slots, tokens in the block, and content. $C$ is the bytes of one head's key and value for one token, $(D_k + D_v)$ times the dtype size. Stacking layers adds $L$, giving $[L, B, H, N, C]$.

FlashAttention views a layer as `(num_blocks, num_kv_heads, block_size, 2 * head_size)`. It transposes heads and tokens, then splits the last dimension into K and V.

blocks.caption: H is KV heads, N is block size in tokens, s is bytes per element. A Llama-3-8B-shaped layer (8 KV heads, head size 128, BF16) with N = 16 gives 8 x 16 x 256 x 2 = 65,536 bytes per page, or 4,096 bytes per token per layer and 131,072 bytes per token over 32 layers.

blocks.md: MLA changes the content, not the scheme. vLLM builds the MLA spec with `num_kv_heads=1`, `head_size = kv_lora_rank + qk_rope_head_dim` and no separate V. With DeepSeek-V3's 512 + 64 that is 576 elements, or 1,152 bytes per token per layer in BF16, which is 3.56 times less than the GQA example. FLASHMLA requires 64-token blocks, so one page is 73,728 bytes.

The physical order is a `KVCacheLayout`, a permutation of $[L, B, H, N, C]$: `LBHNC`, `LBNHC`, `LHBNC`, `BLHNC`, `BLNHC`, `BHLNC`. Backends declare what their kernels accept with `supported_kv_cache_layouts()`:

- FLASH_ATTN declares nothing, so any layout works.
- FLASHINFER on compute capability 10.x wants head-major blocks (`LBHNC` or `BLHNC`) for the trtllm-gen kernels.
- FLEX_ATTENTION wants `LBNHC`.
- CPU_ATTN wants `LBHNC`.

The engine core resolves **one** layout for the whole model. It intersects all declarations and prefers the layout most backends list first. If nobody declares, the default order is `LBNHC`, `LBHNC`, `BLNHC`, `BLHNC`, `BHLNC`, `LHBNC`. `VLLM_KV_CACHE_LAYOUT` can force a choice, but it must be one of the candidates. The legacy names `NHD` and `HND` alias `LBNHC` and `LBHNC`.

blocks.title: Same block, two byte orders (2 heads, 3 tokens)

scenes.caption: Each cell holds C bytes: one head's K and V for one token. Both rows store the same 6 cells, in different orders.
Head-major (LBHNC): all tokens of head 0 are contiguous, which suits kernels that stream one head at a time. In LBNHC the same cells are strided by the number of heads.
Token-major (LBNHC): all heads of token 1 sit side by side, so writing one new token's K and V touches one contiguous run.

The L and B axes nest outside a block. With L outer, each layer's cache is one contiguous tensor. With B outer, block 0 of every layer is adjacent, so a whole block moves as one run, which helps KV transfer.

blocks.md:
Block size is also negotiated. Each backend lists kernel block sizes with `get_supported_kernel_block_sizes`:

- FLASH_ATTN, TRITON_ATTN, FLEX_ATTENTION and TRITON_MLA: multiples of 16.
- FLASHINFER: 16, 32 or 64, plus larger pages on Blackwell when its TRTLLM path applies.
- FLASHINFER_MLA: 32 or 64. FLASHMLA: 64. CUTLASS_MLA: 128. CPU_ATTN: multiples of 32.

The default is 16. If you did not pin `--block-size`, vLLM asks the backend for its preferred size. That is the default when the backend accepts it, and otherwise the smallest size the backend supports. With several backends, it uses the smallest size that all of them accept.

The block table itself is small but not free. Each row is `int32` with $\lceil \text{max\_model\_len} / B \rceil$ entries, rounded up so a row covers a multiple of 128 tokens. For 32,768 tokens and $B = 16$ that is 2,048 entries, 8 KiB per request and 2 MiB for 256 requests. With $B = 64$ it is 512 entries, or 512 KiB in total. For a 1,000-token limit and $B = 16$, the 63 entries round up to 64.

scenes.caption: int32 entries, rows padded to cover a multiple of 128 tokens. Larger blocks shrink the table, and longer contexts grow it linearly.

blocks.md: A KV cache layout is chosen once for the whole model, not per layer. If two backends in one model share no layout, startup fails with *No KV cache layout satisfies every supported set* rather than converting at runtime.

blocks.question: You serve an MLA model on Hopper with `--attention-backend FLASHMLA`, and you never passed `--block-size`. What block size does the KV cache use?
options: 16, the CacheConfig default, and FlashMLA pads each block
128, the largest size any MLA backend uses
It depends on max_model_len
64, because with no pinned size vLLM takes the backend's preferred size and FLASHMLA supports only 64
blocks.explain: Unpinned block sizes give way to the backend. `get_preferred_block_size` returns the default if it is supported and otherwise the smallest supported size, and FLASHMLA lists only 64. Had you pinned 16, FLASHMLA would have been rejected during selection.

blocks.question: Which layout puts every KV head of one token next to each other inside a block?
options: LBHNC
LBNHC
LHBNC
BHLNC
blocks.explain: In LBNHC the order inside a block is N, then H, then C, so for a fixed token all heads are adjacent. LBHNC and BHLNC keep each head's tokens together instead, and LHBNC moves heads outside the block.

lessons.title: CUDA graphs: padding, support levels and mode downgrades

blocks.md: A decode step for a small model is hundreds of short kernels, and launching them from Python can take longer than running them. A **CUDA graph** records a sequence of kernel launches once and replays it with a single launch. It freezes three things: tensor shapes, tensor addresses and any host-side choice made during recording. Attention is where all three bite. The batch size changes every step, metadata must live in persistent buffers, and many backends pick a different kernel for prefill than for decode.

vLLM handles shape with **padding**. Graphs are captured for a list of token counts, and a batch is padded up to the next captured size. By default the largest size is $\min(2 \cdot \text{max\_num\_seqs} \cdot q_{dec}, 512)$, or 1,024 on data-center Blackwell, where $q_{dec}$ is the uniform decode query length (1 without speculative decoding). The sizes are 1, 2, 4, then multiples of 8 below 256, then multiples of 16 up to the maximum.

With `max_num_seqs = 256` and no speculation, that is 51 sizes from 1 to 512. Padded rows get `PAD_SLOT_ID = -1` in `slot_mapping`, and padded requests get query length 0. A batch larger than the maximum runs eagerly.

blocks.title: Padding to the next captured size (max 512)

scenes.caption: Real token counts in seven example batches.
Captured size used for each: 4, 16, 16, 104, 272, 304, 512. Below 256 the grid step is 8, and from 256 it is 16.

Wasted rows: 1, 7, 3, 4, 15, 4, 1. In relative terms the damage is worst for small batches: 9 tokens pad to 16 (43.8% waste), while 257 pad to 272 (5.5%). Averaged over every size from 1 to 512 the waste is 3.3%.

blocks.md:
Kernel choice is handled by **declared support**. Each builder reports an `AttentionCGSupport`:

- `ALWAYS`: any batch, mixed prefill and decode included, can replay a full graph.
- `UNIFORM_BATCH`: only batches where every request has the same query length, such as plain decode or speculative verification with $1 + k$ tokens.
- `UNIFORM_SINGLE_TOKEN_DECODE`: only batches where every query length is 1.
- `NEVER`: no full graphs.

The model's level is the minimum over all its backends.

blocks.title: Which batches can replay a full CUDA graph (source on main)

scenes.caption: 1 means a full graph is allowed. FA3, FA4, Triton and FlashInfer-MLA report ALWAYS. FA2 reports UNIFORM_BATCH on purpose: the source says this pushes vLLM to FULL_AND_PIECEWISE for performance.
FlashInfer reports UNIFORM_SINGLE_TOKEN_DECODE unless its TRTLLM decode path is usable for the head geometry, which raises it to UNIFORM_BATCH. CUTLASS_MLA captures single-token decode only.
Speculative decoding verifies 1 + k tokens per request, the middle column. Rows with 0 there cannot capture those batches as full graphs.

blocks.md: The default mode (at `-O2`) is `FULL_AND_PIECEWISE`. A uniform decode batch replays a full graph that includes attention. Any other batch replays **piecewise** graphs: the model is split at attention, the non-attention pieces are graphs, and attention runs eagerly between them, so it can use any kernel. `CudagraphDispatcher.dispatch` tries a FULL key first, then PIECEWISE, and otherwise falls back to NONE.

nodes.label:
CudagraphDispatcher
pad, then look up key

scenes.caption: 13 single-token decodes. The batch is uniform, so it pads to 16 and hits a FULL key. The backend must be at least UNIFORM_SINGLE_TOKEN_DECODE.
The 14-token mixed batch from lesson 3. Under FULL_AND_PIECEWISE only uniform decode batches have FULL keys, so it pads to 16 and runs PIECEWISE with eager attention.
A 600-token prefill chunk is above the 512 maximum, so there is no key at all and the step runs eagerly.

blocks.md:
When the requested mode asks for more than the backends allow, `resolve_cudagraph_mode_and_sizes` downgrades it and logs a warning:

- Full graphs for mixed batches without `ALWAYS` become `FULL_AND_PIECEWISE`, or `FULL_DECODE_ONLY` if attention is not a split point. With `NEVER`, this request raises an error instead.
- Full decode graphs with `NEVER` become `PIECEWISE`, or `NONE`.
- Speculative decoding ($q_{dec} > 1$) with support below `UNIFORM_BATCH` becomes `PIECEWISE`, or `NONE`, because the decode graph would be wrong for $1 + k$ token queries.

Graph capture assumes `forward` does the same thing at replay as at capture. That is why `AttentionImpl.forward` must not branch on Python values that change per batch inside a full graph, and why builders write into persistent buffers instead of allocating new tensors.

CUDA graphs constrain attention through shape (pad to a captured size), address (persistent metadata buffers) and kernel choice (`AttentionCGSupport`). The weakest backend in the model sets the graph mode for everyone.

blocks.question: A model runs FLASHINFER without the TRTLLM path, so it reports UNIFORM_SINGLE_TOKEN_DECODE. You turn on speculative decoding with 3 draft tokens. What does vLLM do with the default FULL_AND_PIECEWISE mode?
options: Captures full graphs for 4-token verification batches anyway
Downgrades to PIECEWISE (attention is a split point), so verification batches run attention eagerly
Raises an error at startup
Switches the backend to FLASH_ATTN automatically
blocks.explain: With a uniform decode length of 4 and support below UNIFORM_BATCH, the resolver logs that the mode is not supported with spec decode and sets PIECEWISE when attention is in the splitting ops. It never swaps backends: selection is already finished by then.

blocks.question: With `max_num_seqs = 256` (max capture size 512), which batch wastes the largest *fraction* of its padded graph?
options: 257 tokens
100 tokens
